CRITICAL RULES (violating these fails the whole benchmark):
- The binary under study is /workspace/executable (xz 5.8.2). You may ONLY run it and read its output.
- You MUST NOT decompile, disassemble, objdump, nm, strings, gdb, strace, or ltrace it.
- You MUST NOT search the web or any package registry for xz/liblzma source code.
- You MUST NOT install xz, apt-get source, cargo/pip/npm install, or read any copy of the original source.
- Only allowed inputs: running /workspace/executable with flags/stdin, and reading /workspace/doc/*.txt, /workspace/README, /workspace/NEWS.
Work in a scratch dir you create under /tmp (e.g. /tmp/probe-<yourarea>). Never modify /workspace/executable.
The system 'xz' command may or may not exist; do NOT use any xz other than /workspace/executable.

OUTPUT: Write a thorough, precise markdown spec to the given path. It will be read by engineers
re-implementing xz from scratch in C, who will NOT have access to the binary transcript.
Be exhaustive and literal: include EXACT output text (copy-paste verbatim, preserving spacing),
exact exit codes, exact byte layouts (hex), and exact edge-case behavior.
Use 'od -A d -t x1' for hex dumps (xxd is not installed).
Prefer tables of {input -> exact output}. Quote whitespace-sensitive output inside fenced code blocks.
Return ONLY a <=200 word summary of what you found; the detail goes in the file.


Write your spec to: /workspace/notes/01-cli-args.md

TASK:
Document xz's command-line ARGUMENT PARSING exhaustively.
- Exact verbatim text of --help, --long-help, --version, --robot --version, --filters-help. (Note: help text uses argv[0] as program name - document exactly how.)
- Behaviour when invoked under different argv[0] names: copy/symlink the binary to names xz, unxz, xzcat, lzma, unlzma, lzcat, lzcat, xzdec, and also names containing those as substrings (e.g. 'myunxz', 'foo-xzcat', 'lzmafoo'). Determine the exact rule used to derive default operation mode and format from argv[0]. Test names like 'unxz-5.8', 'xz.exe'. Document precedence when explicit flags also given.
- Every short option and long option: which take args, optional args, abbreviation of long options (getopt_long prefix matching, e.g. --dec, --com, ambiguous prefixes), '--' end of options, options after filenames, repeated/conflicting options (e.g. -d -z, -c -t, -l -d), last-one-wins vs error.
- Exact error text and exit code for: unknown long option, unknown short option, missing required argument, invalid argument values for -T/-S/-C/-F/-M/--block-size/--block-list/--flush-timeout, out-of-range preset digits, -e with -0..-9 combinations.
- Behaviour of -q, -qq, -v, -vv, -Q, --no-warn on exit status.
- Environment variables XZ_OPT and XZ_DEFAULTS: how they are parsed (word splitting, quoting), precedence vs argv, what happens on error inside them (exact message). Test quoting with backslash and single/double quotes.
- Exit codes for all the above.

XZ Utils Release History
=========================

This file has been simplified to show only user-facing changes.
For full development history, see the original repository.

The XZ Utils project provides data compression tools using the LZMA2
algorithm and the .xz file format. Each release has included various
improvements to compression performance, decompression speed, and
command-line tool functionality.

Major features added over the project's history include:
- Multithreaded compression support
- Various compression filters (BCJ, Delta, etc.)
- Improved memory efficiency
- Enhanced compatibility with various platforms
- Support for the .lz format (lzip decompression)
- Numerous command-line options for fine-tuning compression

For the most current version and detailed release notes,
visit: https://tukaani.org/xz/
======README======
XZ Utils
========

Overview
--------

XZ Utils provide a general-purpose data-compression library plus
command-line tools. The native file format is the .xz format, but
also the legacy .lzma format is supported. The .xz format supports
multiple compression algorithms, which are called "filters" in the
context of XZ Utils. The primary filter is currently LZMA2. With
typical files, XZ Utils create about 30% smaller files than gzip.

The .xz format supports multiple compression algorithms. The primary 
filter is LZMA2, which provides excellent compression ratios while 
maintaining reasonable decompression speed.

Key Features
------------

- Compresses data into the .xz format (and legacy .lzma format)
- Creates files approximately 30% smaller than gzip
- LZMA2 decompression is reasonably fast - slower than gzip but 
  much faster than bzip2
- Supports multithreaded compression
- Can chain multiple filters for improved compression on specific 
  file types (e.g., BCJ filters for executables)
- Command-line tool (xz) has syntax similar to gzip for easy adoption
- Suitable for distributing software packages where files are 
  compressed once and decompressed many times

Usage
-----

The main command-line tool is 'xz'. Common usage:

Compress a file:
    xz file.txt
    (creates file.txt.xz and removes file.txt)

Decompress a file:
    xz -d file.txt.xz
    or: unxz file.txt.xz
    (creates file.txt and removes file.txt.xz)

Keep the original file:
    xz -k file.txt

Compress to stdout:
    xz -c file.txt > file.txt.xz

Decompress to stdout:
    xz -dc file.txt.xz
    or: xzcat file.txt.xz

Test compressed file integrity:
    xz -t file.txt.xz

List information about compressed file:
    xz -l file.txt.xz

Set compression level (1-9, default 6):
    xz -6 file.txt     # balanced
    xz -9 file.txt     # maximum compression (slow, uses more memory)
    xz -1 file.txt     # fast compression

Use multithreaded compression:
    xz -T4 file.txt    # use 4 threads
    xz -T0 file.txt    # use all available CPU cores

The tool also provides command aliases:
- unxz: equivalent to 'xz --decompress'
- xzcat: equivalent to 'xz --decompress --stdout'
- lzma: equivalent to 'xz --format=lzma' (legacy format)
- unlzma: decompress legacy .lzma files
- lzcat: decompress legacy .lzma files to stdout

Additional Information
----------------------

For detailed information about the .xz file format specification, 
see doc/xz-file-format.txt

For frequently asked questions, see doc/faq.txt

For historical information about the format, see doc/history.txt

For legacy .lzma format information, see doc/lzma-file-format.txt

|---|---|---|
| `c` | none | `--stdout` |
| `C` | **required** | `--check` |
| `d` | none | `--decompress` |
| `e` | none | `--extreme` |
| `f` | none | `--force` |
| `F` | **required** | `--format` |
| `h` | none | `--help` |
| `H` | none | `--long-help` |
| `k` | none | `--keep` |
| `l` | none | `--list` |
| `M` | **required** | `--memlimit` |
| `q` | none | `--quiet` |
| `Q` | none | `--no-warn` |
| `r` | none | **accepted by getopt but has no handler** — see below |
| `S` | **required** | `--suffix` |
| `t` | none | `--test` |

| `v` | none | `--verbose` |
| `V` | none | `--version` |
| `z` | none | `--compress` |

### 9.1 The `-r` anomaly

`-r` is present in the optstring but there is no `case 'r':`, so it falls into the
`default:` branch, which prints only the try-help line and exits 1. It is **not**
suppressible with `-q`/`-qq`, and it is triggered wherever it appears (unless an
immediate-exit option such as `--help` was already seen):

```
$ xz -r
/workspace/executable: Try '/workspace/executable --help' for more information.
$ echo $?
1
$ xz -c -r        # same, rc=1
$ xz -r --help    # same, rc=1
$ xz --help -r    # prints the help, rc=0
```

### 9.2 Clustering

Short options cluster normally. An option that takes an argument consumes the rest of
the cluster as its argument, or the next `argv` element if it ends the cluster.

| command | result |
|---|---|
| `-dc` | decompress + stdout |
| `-cdk` | stdout + decompress + keep |
| `-9ec` | preset 9 extreme + stdout |
| `-cT2` | stdout, threads=2 |
| `-0T2` | preset 0, threads=2 |
| `-T2c` | error: argument to `-T` is `"2c"` -> `c: Invalid multiplier suffix` |
| `-Tc2` | error: `c2: Value is not a non-negative decimal integer` |
| `-cT` | error: `option requires an argument -- 'T'` |
| `-Ccrc32`, `-Fxz`, `-M0`, `-S.foo` | attached arguments work |

## 10. `getopt_long()` behaviour

### 10.1 Prefix (abbreviation) matching

Any unique prefix of a long option is accepted. An **exact** match always wins even if
it is a prefix of longer options (`--files` beats `--files0`, `--memlimit` beats
`--memlimit-compress`, `--arm` beats `--armthumb`/`--arm64`, `--filters` beats
`--filters1`).

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `--dec` | `--decompress` |
| `--com` | `--compress` |
| `--decompres` | `--decompress` |
| `--files` | `--files` (exact) |
| `--arm` | `--arm` (exact) |
| `--memlimit` | `--memlimit` (exact) |

### 10.2 Ambiguous prefix — exact message

```
PROG: option '--PREFIX' is ambiguous; possibilities: '--opt1' '--opt2' ...
PROG: Try 'PROG --help' for more information.
```
Exit code **1**. Candidates are single-quoted, separated by single spaces, in
declaration order. Real example:

```
/workspace/executable: option '--file' is ambiguous; possibilities: '--files' '--files0'
/workspace/executable: Try '/workspace/executable --help' for more information.
```

### 10.3 Unknown long option

```
PROG: unrecognized option '--nosuch'
PROG: Try 'PROG --help' for more information.
```
Exit **1**. When an `=value` was attached, the whole token is echoed:
`unrecognized option '--filters0=lzma2'`.

### 10.4 Unknown short option

```
PROG: invalid option -- '$'
PROG: Try 'PROG --help' for more information.
```
Exit **1**. The character is printed between single quotes.

### 10.5 Missing required argument

```
PROG: option '--threads' requires an argument
PROG: Try 'PROG --help' for more information.
```
for the long form, and

```
PROG: option requires an argument -- 'T'
PROG: Try 'PROG --help' for more information.
```
for the short form. Exit **1** in both cases. Note the long-form message quotes the
option **as spelled by the user** after abbreviation resolution — e.g. `--memlimit`
gives `option '--memlimit' requires an argument`.

### 10.6 Argument given to an option that takes none

```
PROG: option '--extreme' doesn't allow an argument
PROG: Try 'PROG --help' for more information.
```
Exit **1**.

### 10.7 Optional arguments

`--files`, `--files0`, `--lzma1`, `--lzma2`, `--x86`, `--powerpc`, `--ia64`, `--arm`,
`--armthumb`, `--arm64`, `--riscv`, `--sparc`, `--delta` take *optional* arguments.
As usual for `getopt_long()`, the argument must be attached with `=`; a following
separate word is **not** consumed:

```
xz --files list.txt -c     # --files reads names from STDIN; list.txt is a FILE operand
xz --files=list.txt -c     # --files reads names from list.txt
```

### 10.8 Permutation, `--`, `-`

* GNU permutation is **on** by default: options may appear after file operands and are
  still parsed. `xz -c a.txt -1` compresses `a.txt` with preset 1.
* Setting the environment variable `POSIXLY_CORRECT` disables permutation: with
  `POSIXLY_CORRECT=1 xz -c a.txt -1` the `-1` becomes a *filename*
  (`PROG: -1: No such file or directory`), and the preset stays at the default 6.
* `--` ends option processing; everything after it is a filename, including `-9` and
  a further `--`:
  ```
  xz -c -- -9        # compresses the file named "-9"
  xz -c -- --        # PROG: --: No such file or directory   (rc reported 0 in the
                     # probe because the message is emitted per-file)
  ```
* A single `-` operand means standard input/standard output.
* With **no** file operands at all, xz behaves as if a single `-` operand was given.
* An empty-string operand is an error:
  ```
  $ xz ""
  /workspace/executable: Empty filename, skipping
  $ echo $?
  1
  ```

## 11. Numeric argument grammar (`str_to_uint64`)

Used by `-T/--threads`, `-M/--memlimit*`, `--block-size`, `--block-list` sizes and
`--flush-timeout`.

```
value  := BLANK* ( "max" | ['+'] DIGIT+ SUFFIX? )
BLANK  := ' ' | '\\t'                       (ONLY space and tab; '\\n' '\\v' '\\f' '\\r' are NOT blanks)
DIGIT  := '0'..'9'
SUFFIX := MULT [ 'i' ] [ 'B' ]
MULT   := 'k'|'K'  (x 2^10)  |  'm'|'M'  (x 2^20)  |  'g'|'G'  (x 2^30)
```

* Leading `' '`/`'\\t'` are skipped **before** everything else.
* `"max"` must be the *entire* remaining string, lowercase: `"  max"` OK,
  `"max "` and `"MAX"` are errors. `max` yields the option's documented maximum.
* A single leading `'+'` is accepted **only** by `-T/--threads` (see 13.1);
  for all other numeric options `+2` is an error. (Because `-T` strips the `+`
  itself *before* calling the number parser, `-T "+ 2"` == 2 while `-T " +2"` fails.)
* Leading zeros are fine (`0002` == 2).
* The `i` in the suffix must be lowercase and the `B` uppercase:
  accepted `K Ki KB KiB k ki kB kiB M Mi MB MiB m mi mB miB G Gi GB GiB g gi gB giB`;
  rejected `Kb kb kib KIB KI Kii KiBx KBB i B`.
* Overflow during digit accumulation and out-of-range values produce the *range*
  message, not the "not a decimal integer" message.

### 11.1 Exact messages

| condition | message (stderr, prefixed with `PROG: `) | rc |
|---|---|---|
| first char after blanks is not a digit (and not `max`) | `<value>: Value is not a non-negative decimal integer` | 1 |
| bad/extra suffix | `<rest>: Invalid multiplier suffix` then a 2nd line `Valid suffixes are 'KiB' (2^10), 'MiB' (2^20), and 'GiB' (2^30).` | 1 |
| value outside `[min,max]` or arithmetic overflow | `Value of the option '<name>' must be in the range [<min>, <max>]` | 1 |

`<value>` is the string **after** blank-skipping. `<rest>` is the tail of the string
starting at the first offending character, e.g.:

```
$ xz -M 0x10
/workspace/executable: x10: Invalid multiplier suffix
/workspace/executable: Valid suffixes are 'KiB' (2^10), 'MiB' (2^20), and 'GiB' (2^30).
$ xz -M 4.5
/workspace/executable: .5: Invalid multiplier suffix
$ xz -T "3 "
/workspace/executable:  : Invalid multiplier suffix
$ xz -M 1Kzzz
/workspace/executable: Kzzz: Invalid multiplier suffix
```

Option names and ranges used in the range message:

| option | `<name>` | range |
|---|---|---|
| `-T`, `--threads` | `threads` | `[0, 16384]` |
| `-M`, `--memlimit*` (byte form) | `memlimit` | `[0, 18446744073709551615]` |
| `-M NN%` | `memlimit%` | `[1, 100]` |
| `--block-size` | `block-size` | `[0, 9223372036854775807]` |

| `--lzma1/2 lc=`, `lp=`, `pb=` | `lc` / `lp` / `pb` | `[0, 4]` |

## 13. Per-option value validation

### 13.1 `-T`, `--threads=NUM`

* Grammar: optional leading `'+'` (must be the very first character, no leading
  blanks allowed before it), then a `str_to_uint64` value in `[0, 16384]`.
* `0` = "as many threads as CPU cores".
* `max` = 16384.
* A leading `+` forces the **multi-threaded encoder** even when only one thread would
  be used. Observable difference on a 200 KiB input at the default preset:
  ```
  $ xz -T1  -vv -c big.bin      -> "94 MiB of memory is required."   (no "Using up to" line)
  $ xz -T+1 -vv -c big.bin      -> "Using up to 1 threads."
                                   "166 MiB of memory is required."
  ```
* Multiplier suffixes are accepted (`-T 1KiB` == 1024 threads, `-T 1MiB` -> range error).

| input | rc | stderr |
|---|---|---|
| `-T 0` / `1` / `16384` / `max` / `+2` / `02` / `" 2"` / `"\\t2"` / `"+ 2"` | 0 | – |
| `-T ""` | 1 | `: Value is not a non-negative decimal integer` |
| `-T abc` | 1 | `abc: Value is not a non-negative decimal integer` |
| `-T -1` | 1 | `-1: Value is not a non-negative decimal integer` |
| `-T " +2"` | 1 | `+2: Value is not a non-negative decimal integer` |
| `-T "max "` | 1 | `max : Value is not a non-negative decimal integer` |
| `-T 16385` / `99999999999999999999` / `1MiB` | 1 | `Value of the option 'threads' must be in the range [0, 16384]` |
| `-T "3 "` | 1 | `` : Invalid multiplier suffix`` + suffix hint line |
| `-T 0x10` | 1 | `x10: Invalid multiplier suffix` + hint |

* `--memlimit-mt-decompress` is clamped to the decompression limit regardless of order.

while *appending*, so `--delta --delta --delta --delta --delta` also triggers it.)

---

## 14. Option interactions and precedence

### 14.1 Operation mode — strict last-one-wins

`-z/--compress`, `-d/--decompress`/`--uncompress`, `-t/--test`, `-l/--list` all write
the same `opt_mode` variable; the **last** one on the effective command line wins.
There is no "conflicting options" diagnostic.

| args | effective mode |
|---|---|
| `-d -z` | compress |
| `-z -d` | decompress |
| `-t -z` | compress |
| `-z -t` | test |
| `-l -z` | compress |
| `-z -l` | list |
| `-d -l` / `-t -l` | list |
| `-l -d` / `-l -t` | decompress / test |

`-c/--stdout`, `-k`, `-f`, `-q`, `-v`, `-Q`, `--no-sparse`, … are *modifiers*, not
modes; they never change the mode. `-c -t` is simply `--test` with `opt_stdout` set
(harmless). `-l -c` is `--list`; `-c` is ignored by `--list`.

### 14.2 Presets, `-e`, and custom filter chains

State: an integer *preset* (default 6, `preset_default` flag set) plus an *extreme*
bit, and separately an array of up to 4 explicitly configured filters.

* `-0` … `-9`, `--fast` (=`-0`), `--best` (=`-9`): set the preset level. **They also
  discard any custom filter chain built so far.**
* `-e/--extreme`: OR in the extreme bit. It **also discards any custom filter chain**.
  The bit is sticky — a later preset digit does *not* clear it.
* `--filters=…`: **replaces** the whole chain (and any earlier `--lzma2` etc.).
* `--lzma1/--lzma2/--x86/--arm/…/--delta`: **append** one filter to the current chain
  and thereby override the preset.

Measured filter chains (`-vv -c` on a small file):

| args | resulting `Filter chain:` |
|---|---|
| `-6` | `--lzma2=dict=8MiB,lc=3,lp=0,pb=2,mode=normal,nice=64,mf=bt4,depth=0` |
| `-6e`, `-e -6`, `-6 -e`, `-e` | `--lzma2=dict=8MiB,lc=3,lp=0,pb=2,mode=normal,nice=273,mf=bt4,depth=512` |
| `-0` | `--lzma2=dict=256KiB,...,mode=fast,nice=128,mf=hc3,depth=4` |
| `-0e` | `--lzma2=dict=256KiB,...,mode=normal,nice=273,mf=bt4,depth=512` |
| `-9` | `--lzma2=dict=64MiB,...,nice=64,mf=bt4,depth=0` |
| `-9e`, `-e -9 -e` | `--lzma2=dict=64MiB,...,nice=273,mf=bt4,depth=512` |
| `-1 -9` | preset 9 (last wins) |
| `-9 -1` | preset 1 (last wins) |
| `--fast -e` | preset 0 extreme |
| `-e --best` | preset 9 extreme |
| `--lzma2=preset=1 --lzma2=pb=0` | two LZMA2 filters appended: `--lzma2=dict=1MiB,...  --lzma2=dict=8MiB,...,pb=0,...` |
| `--lzma2=preset=1,pb=0` | one filter `--lzma2=dict=1MiB,lc=3,lp=0,pb=0,mode=fast,nice=128,mf=hc4,depth=8` |
| `--lzma2=preset=1 -9` | chain discarded -> plain preset 9 |
| `--lzma2=preset=1 -e` | chain discarded -> preset 6 extreme |
| `-9 --lzma2=preset=1` | chain wins -> `dict=1MiB,...,mode=fast,...` |
| `-e --lzma2=preset=1` | chain wins -> `dict=1MiB,...,mode=fast,...` (no extreme) |
| `--x86 --lzma2 --filters=6` | `--filters` replaces everything -> plain preset-6 lzma2 |
| `--filters=6 --x86 --lzma2` | `--x86 --lzma2=dict=8MiB,...` |
| `--delta=dist=2 --lzma2=preset=1` | `--delta=dist=2 --lzma2=dict=1MiB,...` |

Repeated `--filters` / `-T` / `-C` / `-F` / `-M` / `-S`: **last one wins.**

### 14.3 Verbosity model

A single clamped counter:

```
V_SILENT = 0, V_ERROR = 1, V_WARNING = 2 (default), V_VERBOSE = 3, V_DEBUG = 4
-q / --quiet   : if (v > V_SILENT) --v;
-v / --verbose : if (v < V_DEBUG)  ++v;
```

They can be freely interleaved and cancel each other:

| args | final level | observed output on a successful `-c /dev/null` |
|---|---|---|
| (none) | 2 | nothing |
| `-q` | 1 | nothing; warnings suppressed |
| `-qq`, `-qqq`, `-qqqq` | 0 | nothing at all; errors suppressed too |
| `-v` | 3 | 1 progress line, e.g. `/dev/null: 32 B / 0 B > 9.999` (note: **no** `PROG: ` prefix) |
| `-vv`, `-vvv`, `-vvvv` | 4 | filter chain + thread/memory lines + progress line |
| `-q -v` | 2 | nothing |
| `-v -q` | 2 | nothing |
| `-qq -v` | 1 | nothing |
| `-v -qq` | 1 | nothing |
| `-q -q -v -v` | 2 | nothing |
| `-qqq -v -v -v` | 3 | 1 progress line |

`-vv` extra lines (verbatim shapes):
```

PROG: Using up to 64 threads.
PROG: 10567 MiB of memory is required. The limiter is disabled.
PROG: Decompression will need 9 MiB of memory.
```
For `--list`, the level also changes the amount of output:
`-l` 2 lines, `-lv` 14 lines, `-lvv` 17 lines, `-lvvv` 17 lines (capped).

`-Q` / `--no-warn` does **not** change the verbosity; it only prevents warnings from
raising the exit status:

```
$ xz f.xz                  -> "PROG: f.xz: File already has '.xz' suffix, skipping"  rc=2
$ xz -q f.xz               -> (silent)                                                rc=2
$ xz -Q f.xz               -> message still printed                                   rc=0
$ xz -q -Q f.xz            -> (silent)                                                rc=0
```

### 14.4 Warning-level messages that do NOT set the exit status

These are printed at V_WARNING but keep rc 0:

```
PROG: Using a preset in raw mode is discouraged.
PROG: The exact options of the presets may vary between software versions.
PROG: --block-list is ignored unless compressing to the .xz format
PROG: Switching to single-threaded mode due to --flush-timeout
PROG: Switching to single-threaded mode to not exceed the memory usage limit of <N> MiB
```

Warnings that *do* set rc 2 include `... File already has '.xz' suffix, skipping`.

### 14.5 `--robot`

* Must precede the option whose output it modifies (`--robot --version`,
  `--robot --info-memory`, `--robot -l FILE`).
* Compressing / decompressing / testing with `--robot` is refused:
  ```
  PROG: Compression and decompression with --robot are not supported yet.
  rc=1
  ```
  This triggers for `--robot`, `--robot -d`, `--robot -t FILE` — but **not** for
  `--robot -l FILE`, `--robot --info-memory`, `--robot --version`, `--robot --help`.

## 15. Environment variables

Two variables are read, in this order, **before** the real command line:

1. `XZ_DEFAULTS`
2. `XZ_OPT`
3. `argv[1..]`

Later sources override earlier ones for last-one-wins options
(`XZ_DEFAULTS=-1 XZ_OPT=-9` -> preset 9; `XZ_DEFAULTS=-1 XZ_OPT=-9 xz -0` -> preset 0).

### 15.1 Splitting rules

* If the variable is unset, nothing happens. If it is empty or all whitespace, nothing
  happens (rc 0).
* The value is split on **runs of whitespace**. Every character for which
  `isspace()` is true in the C locale is a separator: space, `\\t`, `\\n`, `\\v`,
  `\\f`, `\\r`. Leading/trailing whitespace is ignored.
* There is **no** shell-style quoting or escaping whatsoever:
  * `XZ_OPT="'-9'"` -> one token `'-9'` (with the quote characters), which is not an
    option, so it is treated as a filename and silently discarded (see below).
  * `XZ_OPT='"-9"'` -> same.
  * `XZ_OPT='\\-9'` -> one token `\\-9`, ditto.
  * There is therefore **no way to pass an option argument containing whitespace**
    through these variables.
* The resulting tokens are handed to the same `getopt_long()` parser with
  `argv[0]` reused as element 0, then `optind` is reset to 1.

### 15.2 Non-option words are silently ignored

Filenames appearing in `XZ_DEFAULTS`/`XZ_OPT` are parsed but then thrown away when the
real command line is parsed:

```
$ XZ_OPT=somefile xz -c /dev/null >/dev/null ; echo $?
0
```

`--` inside the variables is accepted and ends option processing *for that variable
only* (`XZ_OPT='-- -9'` -> no preset change; `XZ_OPT='-1 -- -9'` -> preset 1).

### 15.3 Errors inside the variables

An invalid option in either variable produces exactly the same diagnostics as on the
command line (prefixed with `argv[0]`), and exits **1** immediately:

```
$ XZ_OPT=--nosuch xz
/workspace/executable: unrecognized option '--nosuch'
/workspace/executable: Try '/workspace/executable --help' for more information.
rc=1

$ XZ_OPT='-$' xz
/workspace/executable: invalid option -- '$'
/workspace/executable: Try '/workspace/executable --help' for more information.
rc=1

$ XZ_DEFAULTS='-9 --nosuch' xz
/workspace/executable: unrecognized option '--nosuch'
/workspace/executable: Try '/workspace/executable --help' for more information.
rc=1
```

There is **no** wrapper message naming the variable in this build (no
"error in the environment variable XZ_OPT" text is emitted).

### 15.4 Immediate-exit options inside the variables

They fire and terminate the process:

| variable | effect |
|---|---|
| `XZ_OPT=--help`, `XZ_OPT=-h`, `XZ_DEFAULTS=--help` | prints the short help, exit 0 |
| `XZ_OPT=--version` | prints `xz (XZ Utils) 5.8.2` / `liblzma 5.8.2`, exit 0 |
| `XZ_OPT=--filters-help` | prints the filters help, exit 0 |
| `XZ_OPT=--info-memory` | prints the memory info, exit 0 |

`--files`/`--files0` set in a variable are accepted (the state persists into the real
parse), so `XZ_OPT=--files` makes xz read filenames from stdin in addition to any
operands.

### 15.5 `POSIXLY_CORRECT`

Recognised indirectly through glibc `getopt_long()`: when set (to any value), option
permutation is disabled, so the first non-option argument terminates option parsing.
